title: حِكَايَةُ الْعَاشِقِ وَالْمَعْشُوقِ
titleEn: The Lover and the Beloved, continued
part: Night 124 · The Lover and the Beloved, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 599–601 (Night 124, continuing directly from nights-123), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 124 continues the story that the vizier Dandān tells within the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, the story of the lover, the beloved and the go-between. ʿAzīz goes on with his tale to Tāj al-Mulūk. The marriage contract signed and the witnesses gone, the young woman takes him to bed, and the night is told frankly, with a ribald verse. In the morning she tells him the house is opened only one day a year: he stays a full year with her, and she bears him a son. When the door opens again she lets him go out at nightfall only after he swears to return that same night, and he goes first to the garden where he used to meet the lady he once visited. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الرَّابِعَةُ وَالْعِشْرُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-rābiʿatu wa-al-ʿishrūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fourth and the twenty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and twenty-fourth night,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الشَّابَّ قَالَ لِتَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ فَلَمَّا كَتَبُوا الْكِتَابَ أَشْهَدَتْ عَلَى نَفْسِهَا أَنَّهَا قَبَضَتْ جَمِيعَ الْمَهْرِ مُقَدَّمًا وَمُؤَخَّرًا وَأَنَّ لِي فِى ذِمَّتِهَا عَشَرَةَ آلَافِ دِرْهَمٍ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-shābba qāla li-tāji al-mulūki fa-lammā katabū al-kitāba ashhadat ʿalā nafsihā annahā qabaḍat jamīʿa al-mahri muqaddaman wa-muʾakhkharan wa-anna lī fī dhimmatihā ʿasharata ālāfi dirhamin
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that the youth said to Tāj al-Mulūk: And when they wrote the writ, she made-witness against herself that she had received all of the dower, advanced and deferred, and that for me in her charge (are) ten thousands (of) dirham.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the young man said to Tāj al-Mulūk: When they had written out the contract, she declared before the witnesses that she had received the whole of the dower, both the part due at once and the part deferred, and that she owed me ten thousand dirhams.
sentences.n: Shahrazād picks the story up by repeating the end of the last night. muqaddaman wa-muʾakhkharan, “advanced and deferred”: the two parts of the dower, here as adverbial accusatives, “(both) in advance and deferred”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا أَعْطَتِ الشُّهُودَ أُجْرَتَهُمْ وَانْصَرَفُوا مِنْ حَيْثُ أَتَوْا
sentences.tr: thumma innahā aʿṭati al-shuhūda ujratahum wa-inṣarafū min ḥaythu ataw
sentences.l: Then she gave the witnesses their fee, and they went-off from where they had come.
sentences.i: Then she paid the witnesses their fee, and they went back the way they had come.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ قَامَتِ الصَّبِيَّةُ وَقَلَعَتْ أَثْوَابَهَا وَأَنَتْ فِي قَمِيصٍ رَفِيعٍ مُطَرَّزٍ بِطِرَازٍ مِنَ الذَّهَبِ وَقَلَعَتْ لِبَاسَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika qāmati al-ṣabiyyatu wa-qalaʿat athwābahā wa-anat fī qamīṣin rafīʿin muṭarrazin bi-ṭirāzin mina al-dhahabi wa-qalaʿat libāsahā
sentences.l: So at that the young-woman stood, and pulled-off her garments, and [came] in a shift, fine, embroidered with an embroidered-border of gold; and she pulled-off her drawers.
sentences.i: At that the young woman rose and took off her clothes, and stood there in a fine shift embroidered with a border of gold; then she took off her drawers.
sentences.n: The print has wa-anat, which makes no sense here. Two readings are possible: wa-atat, “and she came”, which differs only by the dot of one letter, or wa-bānat, “and she appeared”, with a letter lost. Since it cannot be told which, the print is kept and translated by the sense. qalaʿat, “she pulled off”, is the spoken verb for taking off clothes. libās here is a woman’s drawers, the loose trousers worn under the shift. A ṭirāz is an embroidered band, often of gold thread.

sentences.t: وَأَخَذَتْ بِيَدِي وَطَلَعَتْ بِي إِلَى فَوْقِ السَّرِيرِ وَقَالَتْ لِي مَافِى الْحَلَالِ مِنْ عَيْبٍ
sentences.tr: wa-akhadhat bi-yadī wa-ṭalaʿat bī ilā fawqi al-sarīri wa-qālat lī mā fī al-ḥalāli min ʿaybin
sentences.l: And she took by my hand and went-up with me to on-top of the bed, and said to me: There is not in the lawful any shame.
sentences.i: She took me by the hand and climbed with me up onto the bed, and said to me, “There is no shame in what is lawful.”
sentences.n: akhadhat bi-yadī, “she took by my hand”: bi- marks what is grasped. ṭalaʿat bī, “she went up with me”: bi- with a verb of motion means taking someone along. mā fī al-ḥalāl min ʿayb, “there is not, in the lawful, any shame”: min after a negative means “any … at all”. The print runs mā and fī together. al-ḥalāl is what religious law permits — they are now married.

sentences.t: وَنَامَتْ عَلَى السَّرِيرِ وَانْسَطَحَتْ عَلَى ظَهْرِهَا وَرَمَتْنِي عَلَى صَدْرِهَا ثُمَّ شَهَقَتْ شَهْقَةً وَأَتْبَعَتْهَا بِغَنْجَةٍ ثُمَّ كَشَفَتِ الثَّوْبَ إِلَى فَوْقِ نُهُودِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-nāmat ʿalā al-sarīri wa-insaṭaḥat ʿalā ẓahrihā wa-ramatnī ʿalā ṣadrihā thumma shahaqat shahqatan wa-atbaʿathā bi-ghanjatin thumma kashafati al-thawba ilā fawqi nuhūdihā
sentences.l: And she lay on the bed and stretched-flat on her back, and threw me upon her breast; then she gasped a gasp and made-it-follow with a coo, then uncovered the garment to above her breasts.
sentences.i: She lay down on the bed, stretched out on her back, and pulled me down onto her breast; then she gave a gasp and followed it with a languishing coo, and drew her shift up above her breasts.
sentences.n: ghanja is the coquettish, melting sound or manner of a woman making love; atbaʿathā bi-ghanjatin, “she made it follow with a coo”: bi- names what follows. insaṭaḥat, “she lay flat on her back”, is the seventh form of saṭaḥa.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَيْتُهَا عَلَى هَذِهِ الْحَالَةِ لَمْ أَمْلِكْ نَفْسِي دُونَ أَنْ أَوْلَجْتُهُ فِيهَا بَعْدَ أَنْ مَصَصْتُ شَفَتَهَا وَهِيَ تَتَأَوَّهُ وَتُظْهِرُ الْخُشُوعَ وَالْبُكَاءَ مِنْ غَيْرِ دُمُوعٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾaytuhā ʿalā hādhihi al-ḥālati lam amlik nafsī dūna an awlajtuhu fīhā baʿda an maṣaṣtu shafatahā wa-hiya tataʾawwahu wa-tuẓhiru al-khushūʿa wa-al-bukāʾa min ghayri dumūʿin
sentences.l: And when I saw her in this state, I did not master myself short-of that I put-it-in into her, after that I sucked her lip, and she was moaning and showing the submissiveness and the weeping without tears.
sentences.i: When I saw her like that I could not hold myself back, and I put it into her, after I had sucked her lip; and she moaned, and made a show of melting and of weeping without tears.
sentences.n: lam amlik nafsī dūna an awlajtuhu, “I did not master myself short of putting it in”: an with a past tense, as here (and again in baʿda an maṣaṣtu), is good Classical usage for a deed already done: “short of my having put it in”. The pronoun “it” has no noun to refer back to; the reader supplies it. al-khushūʿ is humble surrender; with weeping “without tears” it is the lover’s show of being overcome.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ يَاحَبِيبِي اعْمَلْ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat yā ḥabībī iʿmal
sentences.l: Then she said: O my beloved, do!
sentences.i: Then she said, “Do it, my darling!”
sentences.n: The print runs yā and ḥabībī together.

sentences.t: وَأَذْكَرَتْنِي فِى الْحَالِ قَوْلَ مَنْ قَالَ
sentences.tr: wa-adhkaratnī fī al-ḥāli qawla man qāla
sentences.l: And she reminded me in the moment of the saying of who said:
sentences.i: And at once she put me in mind of the lines of the poet who said:

sentences.t:
وَلَمَا كَشَفْتُ الثَّوْبَ عَنْ سَطْحِ كُسِّهَا * وَجَدْتُ بِهَا ضِيْقًا كَخُلْقِي وَاَرْزَاقِي
فَاَوْلَجْتُ فِيْهَا نِصْفَهُ فَتَنَهَّدَتْ * فَقُلْتُ لِمَا هٰذَا فَقَالَتْ عَلَى الْبَاقِي
sentences.tr:
wa-lamā kashaftu al-thawba ʿan saṭḥi kussihā * wajadtu bihā ḍīqan ka-khulqī wa-arzāqī
fa-awlajtu fīhā niṣfahu fa-tanahhadat * fa-qultu limā hādhā fa-qālat ʿalā al-bāqī
sentences.l:
And when I uncovered the garment from the surface of her cunt, * I found in it a narrowness like my temper and my livelihoods;
so I put-in into her half of it, and she sighed. * So I said: For-what (is) this? So she said: For the remainder.
sentences.i:
When I drew the cloth back from the mound of her cunt, * I found it as narrow as my temper and my means;
I put half of it in, and she sighed. * “What is that sigh for?” I said. “For the rest,” she said.
sentences.n: The joke turns on ḍīq, “narrowness”: a man who is ḍayyiq al-khulq is short-tempered, one who is ḍayyiq al-rizq is hard up, and the poet finds her as tight as both. She sighs not for what she has had but for the half still to come. The print points lamā with a single mīm where lammā, “when”, is meant, and limā for lima, “why”; both are copied as printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ يَا حَبِيبِي اعْمَلْ خَلَاصَكَ فَأَنَا جَارِيَتُكَ خُذْهُ هَاتِهِ كُلَّهُ بِحَيَاتِي عِنْدَكَ هَاتِهِ حَتَّى أُدْخِلَهُ بِيَدِي وَأَحُطَّهُ فِي فُؤَادِي
sentences.tr: thumma qālat yā ḥabībī iʿmal khalāṣaka fa-anā jāriyatuka khudhhu hātihi kullahu bi-ḥayātī ʿindaka hātihi ḥattā udkhilahu bi-yadī wa-aḥuṭṭahu fī fuʾādī
sentences.l: Then she said: O my beloved, do your release, for I (am) your slave-girl; take it — give-it-here, all of it, by my life with you — give-it-here, so that I put-it-in with my hand and set it in my heart.
sentences.i: Then she said, “My darling, take your pleasure to the end — I am your slave-girl. Take it — give it here, all of it, by my life I beg you — give it here, and I will put it in with my own hand and lay it in my heart.”
sentences.n: iʿmal khalāṣaka, “do your release”: finish, come to your climax. hāt, “give here!”, with the object suffix: hātihi. Setting khudhhu, “take it”, right beside it is the muddle of the moment, not a slip. bi-ḥayātī ʿindaka, “by my life with you”, i.e. by the love you bear me: a spoken form of entreaty, bi- of the oath. bi-yadī, “with my hand”: bi- of the instrument.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ تَزَلْ تُسْمِعُنِى الْغُنْجَ وَالْبُكَاءَ وَالشَّهِيقَ فِي خِلَالِ الْبَوْسِ وَالتَّعْنِيقِ حَتَّى صَارَ صِيَاحُنَا فِى الطَّرِيقِ وَحَظِينَا بِالسَّعَادَةِ وَالتَّوْفِيقِ
sentences.tr: wa-lam tazal tusmiʿunī al-ghunja wa-al-bukāʾa wa-al-shahīqa fī khilāli al-bawsi wa-al-taʿnīqi ḥattā ṣāra ṣiyāḥunā fī al-ṭarīqi wa-ḥaẓīnā bi-al-saʿādati wa-al-tawfīqi
sentences.l: And she did not cease making-me-hear the cooing and the weeping and the gasping, in the midst of the kissing and the embracing, until our crying-out became in the street — and we were-favoured with the bliss and the good-success.
sentences.i: And all through the kissing and the clasping she never stopped cooing and weeping and gasping in my ears, until our cries could be heard in the street, and we were granted bliss and fulfilment.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: shahīq, taʿnīq, ṭarīq, tawfīq. al-baws, “kissing”, is the verbal noun of bāsa, yabūsu, “to kiss”, a word taken from Persian; it has nothing to do with buʾs, “misery”. ḥaẓīnā bi-, “we were favoured with”: the verb takes bi- for the thing obtained.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نِمْنَا إِلَى الصَّبَاحِ وَأَرَدْتُ أَنْ أَخْرُجَ وَإِذَا هِيَ أَقْبَلَتْ عَلَيَّ تَضْحَكُ وَتَقُولُ يُوهْ يُوهْ هَلْ تَحْسِبُ أَنْتَ أَنَّ دُخُولَ الْحَمَّامِ مِثْلُ خُرُوجِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma nimnā ilā al-ṣabāḥi wa-aradtu an akhruja wa-idhā hiya aqbalat ʿalayya taḍḥaku wa-taqūlu yūh yūh hal taḥsibu anta anna dukhūla al-ḥammāmi mithlu khurūjihi
sentences.l: Then we slept until the morning, and I wanted to go-out, and behold, she came-toward me laughing and saying: Yoh, yoh! Do you reckon, you, that the entering of the bathhouse (is) like its leaving?
sentences.i: Then we slept till morning. I wanted to go out, but there she was coming toward me, laughing and saying, “Oho! Oho! Do you think going into the bathhouse is the same as coming out of it?
sentences.n: yūh is a spoken cry of surprise or mock dismay. “Going into the bathhouse is not like coming out of it” is a proverb: it is easy to get into a thing, not so easy to get out.

sentences.t: وَمَا أَظُنُّ إِلَّا أَنَّكَ تَحْسِبُنِي مِثْلَ بِنْتِ الدَّلِيلَةِ الْمُحْتَالَةِ إِيَّاكَ وَهَذَا الظَّنَّ
sentences.tr: wa-mā aẓunnu illā annaka taḥsibunī mithla binti al-dalīlati al-muḥtālati iyyāka wa-hādhā al-ẓanna
sentences.l: And I do not think except that you reckon me like the daughter of the Dalīla, the trickster. Beware-you and this thinking!
sentences.i: I can only suppose you take me for the daughter of Dalīla the trickster. Put that thought out of your head!
sentences.n: iyyāka wa-hādhā al-ẓanna, “you — and this thought!”: iyyāka with wa- and an accusative is the Classical formula of warning, “beware of …”.

sentences.t: فَمَا أَنْتَ إِلَّا زَوْجِي بِالْكِتَابِ وَالسُّنَّةِ وَإِنْ كُنْتَ سَكْرَانًا فَاصْحَ لِعَقْلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-mā anta illā zawjī bi-al-kitābi wa-al-sunnati wa-in kunta sakrānan fa-iṣḥa li-ʿaqlika
sentences.l: For you are not except my husband, by the Book and the Sunna; and if you were drunk, then sober-up to your reason!
sentences.i: You are my husband, nothing less, by the Book and the Sunna. If you are drunk, come back to your senses!
sentences.n: bi-al-kitāb wa-al-sunna, “by the Book and the Sunna”: by the Qurʾān and the Prophet’s practice, that is, by a marriage valid in religious law. sakrānan takes the indefinite ending, which the book language does not give this adjective; a Middle Arabic form, as printed. iṣḥa li-ʿaqlika, “wake up to your reason”: li- marks what one comes back to.

sentences.t: إِنَّ هَذِهِ الدَّارَ الَّتِي أَنْتَ فِيهَا مَا تُفْتَحُ إِلَّا فِي كُلِّ سَنَةٍ يَوْمًا
sentences.tr: inna hādhihi al-dāra allatī anta fīhā mā tuftaḥu illā fī kulli sanatin yawman
sentences.l: Indeed this house which you (are) in it is not opened except in every year a day.
sentences.i: This house you are in is opened only one day in every year.

sentences.t: قُمْ وَانْظُرْ إِلَى الْبَابِ الْكَبِيرِ فَقُمْتُ إِلَى الْبَابِ الْكَبِيرِ فَوَجَدْتُهُ مُغْلَقًا مُسَمَّرًا فَعُدْتُ وَأَعْلَمْتُهَا بِأَنَّهُ مُغْلَقٌ مُسَمَّرٌ
sentences.tr: qum wa-unẓur ilā al-bābi al-kabīri fa-qumtu ilā al-bābi al-kabīri fa-wajadtuhu mughlaqan musammaran fa-ʿudtu wa-aʿlamtuhā bi-annahu mughlaqun musammarun
sentences.l: Stand and look at the big door! So I stood (and went) to the big door, and I found it locked, nailed-up; so I returned and informed her that it (was) locked, nailed-up.
sentences.i: Get up and look at the great door.” I got up and went to the great door, and found it locked and nailed shut; so I came back and told her it was locked and nailed shut.
sentences.n: aʿlamtuhā bi-annahu, “I informed her of its being …”: the verb takes bi- for what is told.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لِي يَا عَزِيزُإِنَّ عِنْدَنَا مِنَ الدَّقِيقِ وَالْحُبُوبِ وَالْفَوَاكِهِ وَالرُّمَّانِ وَالسُّكَّرِ وَاللَّحْمِ وَالْغَنَمِ وَالدَّجَاجِ وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ مَا يَكْفِينَا أَعْوَامًا عَدِيدَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lī yā ʿazīzu inna ʿindanā mina al-daqīqi wa-al-ḥubūbi wa-al-fawākihi wa-al-rummāni wa-al-sukkari wa-al-laḥmi wa-al-ghanami wa-al-dajāji wa-ghayri dhālika mā yakfīnā aʿwāman ʿadīdatan
sentences.l: So she said to me: O ʿAzīz, indeed with us, of the flour and the grains and the fruits and the pomegranates and the sugar and the meat and the sheep and the chickens and other-than that, (is) what suffices us years numerous.
sentences.i: She said to me, “ʿAzīz, we have flour and grain and fruit and pomegranates, sugar and meat, sheep and chickens and more besides, enough to last us for years and years.
sentences.n: The print runs the name ʿAzīz and inna together as one word. inna ʿindanā … mā yakfīnā, “indeed with us is what suffices us”: the long list hangs on min, “of”, and mā yakfīnā is the subject.

sentences.t: وَمِنْ هَذِهِ السَّاعَةِ لَا يُفْتَحُ الْبَابُ إِلَّا بَعْدَ سَنَةٍ وَأَنَا أَعْلَمُ أَنَّكَ مَا بَقِيتَ تَرَي رُوحَكَ خَارِجًا عَنْ هَذِهِ الدَّارِ إِلَّا بَعْدَ سَنَةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-min hādhihi al-sāʿati lā yuftaḥu al-bābu illā baʿda sanatin wa-anā aʿlamu annaka mā baqīta tarā rūḥaka khārijan ʿan hādhihi al-dāri illā baʿda sanatin
sentences.l: And from this hour the door is not opened except after a year; and I know that you no-longer see your soul outside of this house except after a year.
sentences.i: From this hour the door will not be opened until a year has passed, and I know you will not see yourself outside this house again until a year is up.”
sentences.n: mā baqīta tarā, “you have not remained seeing”: spoken mā baqā with a present verb means “no longer”, and here looks forward. rūḥaka, “your soul”, is the spoken way of saying “yourself”. The print writes tarā with a final yāʾ.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَاحَوْلَ وَلَاقُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-allāhi
sentences.l: So I said: (There is) no might and no strength except by God.
sentences.i: I said, “There is no might and no strength save in God.”
sentences.n: The formula of resignation in the face of what cannot be helped. bi-allāh, “by God”, “through God”: bi- of the means. The print runs lā and its noun together twice.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ وَأَيُّ شَيْءٍ يَضُرُّكَ وَأَنْتَ تَعْرِفُ صَنْعَةَ الدِّيكِ الَّتِي أَخْبَرْتُكَ بِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat wa-ayyu shayʾin yaḍurruka wa-anta taʿrifu ṣanʿata al-dīki allatī akhbartuka bihā
sentences.l: So she said: And what thing harms you, while you know the craft of the rooster, which I informed you of it?
sentences.i: She said, “And what harm can it do you, when you know the cock’s trade that I told you about?”
sentences.n: akhbartuka bihā, “I informed you of it”: the verb takes bi- for the thing told.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ ضَحِكَتْ فَضَحِكْتُ أَنَا وَطَاوَعْتُهَا فِيمَا قَالَتْ وَمَكَثْتُ عِنْدَهَا وَأَنَا أَعْمَلُ صَنْعَةَ الدِّيكِ آكُلُ وَأَشْرَبُ وَأَنِيكُ حَتَّى مَرَّ عَلَيْنَا عَامٌ اثْنَىْ عَشَرَ شَهْرًا
sentences.tr: thumma ḍaḥikat fa-ḍaḥiktu anā wa-ṭāwaʿtuhā fīmā qālat wa-makathtu ʿindahā wa-anā aʿmalu ṣanʿata al-dīki ākulu wa-ashrabu wa-anīku ḥattā marra ʿalaynā ʿāmun ithnay ʿashara shahran
sentences.l: Then she laughed, and I laughed, I, and I complied-with her in what she said; and I stayed with her, and I doing the craft of the rooster: I eat and drink and fuck — until there passed over us a year, twelve months.
sentences.i: Then she laughed, and I laughed too, and gave in to what she said; and I stayed with her, plying the cock’s trade — eating and drinking and fucking — until a year had gone by over us, twelve whole months.
sentences.n: ithnay ʿashara, “twelve”: the print uses the oblique form ithnay where the nominative ithnā would stand in the book language; a Middle Arabic habit, as printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَمَلَتِ السَّنَةُ حَمَلَتْ مِنِّي وَرُزِقْتُ مِنْهَا وَلَدًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kamalati al-sanatu ḥamalat minnī wa-ruziqtu minhā waladan
sentences.l: And when the year was-complete, she conceived from me, and I was-granted from her a child.
sentences.i: When the year was complete she had conceived by me, and I was blessed with a son by her.
sentences.n: ruziqtu waladan, “I was provided with a child”: the passive of razaqa, God being the giver understood. walad is a child, and most often a son.

sentences.t: وَعِنْدَ رَأْسِ السَّنَةِ سَمِعْتُ فَتْحَ الْبَابِ وَإِذَا بِرِجَالٍ دَخَلُوا بِكَعْكٍ وَدَقِيقٍ وَسُكَّرٍ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿinda raʾsi al-sanati samiʿtu fatḥa al-bābi wa-idhā bi-rijālin dakhalū bi-kaʿkin wa-daqīqin wa-sukkarin
sentences.l: And at the head of the year I heard the opening of the door, and behold, men entered with cakes and flour and sugar.
sentences.i: At the year’s turning I heard the door being opened, and there were men coming in with cakes and flour and sugar.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bi-rijālin, “and behold, men”: after idhā of surprise, bi- only marks what appears. dakhalū bi-kaʿkin, “they came in with cakes”: bi- with a verb of motion means bringing. kaʿk is a ring-shaped biscuit-bread.

sentences.t: فَأَرَدْتُ أَنْ أَخْرُجَ فَقَالَتِ اصْبِرْ إِلَى وَقْتِ الْعِشَاءِ وَمِثْلَ مَادَخَلْتَ فَاخْرُجْ
sentences.tr: fa-aradtu an akhruja fa-qālati iṣbir ilā waqti al-ʿishāʾi wa-mithla mā dakhalta fa-ukhruj
sentences.l: So I wanted to go-out, so she said: Wait until the time of the nightfall, and like what you entered, so go-out!
sentences.i: I wanted to go out, but she said, “Wait until nightfall, and go out the way you came in.”
sentences.n: waqt al-ʿishāʾ, the time of the last prayer of the day, after dark. The print runs mā and dakhalta together.

sentences.t: فَصَبَرْتُ إِلَى وَقْتِ الْعِشَاءِ وَأَرَدْتُ أَنْ أَخْرُجَ وَأَنَا خَائِفٌ مَرْعُوبٌ وَإِذَا هِيَ قَالَتْ وَاللَّهِ مَا أَدَعُكَ تَخْرُجُ حَتَّى أُحَلِّفَكَ أَنَّكَ تَعُودُ فِي هَذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ قَبْلَ أَنْ يُغْلَقَ الْبَابُ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣabartu ilā waqti al-ʿishāʾi wa-aradtu an akhruja wa-anā khāʾifun marʿūbun wa-idhā hiya qālat wa-allāhi mā adaʿuka takhruju ḥattā uḥallifaka annaka taʿūdu fī hādhihi al-laylati qabla an yughlaqa al-bābu
sentences.l: So I waited until the time of the nightfall, and I wanted to go-out, and I (was) fearful, terrified; and behold, she said: By God, I do not let you go-out until I make-you-swear that you return in this night before that the door is locked.
sentences.i: So I waited until nightfall and was about to go out, afraid and terrified, when she said, “By God, I will not let you go until I have made you swear that you will come back this same night before the door is shut.”

sentences.t: فَأَجَبْتُهَا إِلَى ذَلِكَ فَحَلَّفَتْنِي بِالْأَيْمَانِ الْوَثِيقَةِ عَلَى السَّيْفِ وَالْمُصْحَفِ وَالطَّلَاقِ أَنِّي أَعُودُ إِلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-ajabtuhā ilā dhālika fa-ḥallafatnī bi-al-aymāni al-wathīqati ʿalā al-sayfi wa-al-muṣḥafi wa-al-ṭalāqi annī aʿūdu ilayhā
sentences.l: So I answered her to that, and she made-me-swear with the oaths, the binding, upon the sword and the Qurʾān-copy and the divorce, that I return to her.
sentences.i: I agreed to it, and she made me swear the most binding oaths — on the sword, on the Qurʾān, and on pain of divorce — that I would come back to her.
sentences.n: To swear “on divorce” is to swear that, if the oath is broken, one’s wife is divorced; with the sword and the muṣḥaf, a written copy of the Qurʾān, it makes the heaviest of oaths. bi-al-aymān, “with the oaths”: bi- names what one is made to swear.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ خَرَجْتُ مِنْ عِنْدِهَا وَمَضَيْتُ إِلَى الْبُسْتَانِ فَوَجَدْتُهُ مَفْتُوحًا كَعَادَتِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma kharajtu min ʿindihā wa-maḍaytu ilā al-bustāni fa-wajadtuhu maftūḥan ka-ʿādatihi
sentences.l: Then I went-out from her place and went-off to the garden, and I found it open, as its custom (was).
sentences.i: Then I left her and made my way to the garden, and found it open, as it always used to be.
sentences.n: ka-ʿādatihi, “like its custom”: ka- of comparison.

sentences.t: فَاغْتَظْتُ وَقُلْتُ فِي نَفْسِي إِنِّي غَائِبٌ عَنْ هَذَا الْمَكَانِ سَنَةً كَامِلَةً وَجِئْتُهُ عَلَى غَفْلَةٍ فَوَجَدْتُهُ مَفْتُوحًا كَعَادَتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-ightaẓtu wa-qultu fī nafsī innī ghāʾibun ʿan hādhā al-makāni sanatan kāmilatan wa-jiʾtuhu ʿalā ghaflatin fa-wajadtuhu maftūḥan ka-ʿādatihi
sentences.l: So I was-vexed, and I said in myself: I (have been) absent from this place a year, complete, and I came to it at unawareness, and I found it open as its custom.
sentences.i: I was vexed, and said to myself, “I have been away from this place a whole year, and I come back to it unannounced and find it open as it always was.
sentences.n: ʿalā ghaflatin, “upon unawareness”: without warning, when no one was expecting it.

sentences.t: يَا تُرَى هَلِ الصَّبِيَّةُ بَاقِيَةٌ عَلَى حَالِهَا أَوْلَا
sentences.tr: yā turā hali al-ṣabiyyatu bāqiyatun ʿalā ḥālihā aw lā
sentences.l: O, is-it-seen: is the young-woman remaining on her state or not?
sentences.i: I wonder — is the young woman still as she was, or not?
sentences.n: yā turā, “O, is it seen?”, is the spoken “I wonder”. The print runs aw and lā together.

sentences.t: وَلَكِنْ لَا بُدَّ أَنِّي أَدْخُلُ وَأَنْظُرُ قَبْلَ أَنْ أَرُوحَ إِلَى أُمِّي وَأَنَا فِي وَقْتِ الْعِشَاءِ
sentences.tr: wa-lākin lā budda annī adkhulu wa-anẓuru qabla an arūḥa ilā ummī wa-anā fī waqti al-ʿishāʾi
sentences.l: But (there is) no escape that I enter and look, before that I go to my mother, and I (am) in the time of the nightfall.
sentences.i: But I must go in and look before I go to my mother, now that it is nightfall.”
sentences.n: lā budda annī adkhulu, “there is no escape (from) that I enter”: “I must go in”. arūḥa, “I go”: the spoken verb rāḥa.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ دَخَلْتُ الْبُسْتَانَ
sentences.tr: thumma dakhaltu al-bustāna
sentences.l: Then I entered the garden.
sentences.i: Then I went into the garden.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: Morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
